newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU mulls tax on foreign phone, Internet operators.
newsitem.headline: EU mulls tax on foreign phone, Internet operators.

text.p: The European Commission, under pressure from European Union telecommunication firms, is drafting a proposal to force non-EU phone rivals to charge VAT for services offered in Europe.

Industry and Commission sources said on Monday the EU executive was finalising a proposal which would involve levying Value Added Tax on cheap call-back services and calling cards where they are used rather than where they are billed.
Non-European computer online service providers such as America Online would also have to add a VAT charge to the bills of their customers in the EU.

Under the current rules -- adopted in 1977, when international telephone calls where made only through local telecoms operators -- companies based outside the 15-nation bloc do not have to levy VAT on services offered to their EU customers.

Those advocating a new system say that is inconsistent with the increasing use by large companies and business travellers of "call-back" or direct call services offered by new companies at prices significantly lower than those charged by the established telecoms firms.

With "call-back" services, many of which operate out of the United States, a customer making an international call gets a connection by dialing a U.S. number rather than going through the local phone company.
The Commission's initiative to change the 20-year-old directive on VAT on telecoms services was pushed by EU national governments, a Commission official said.

That reflects a twin goal of increasing VAT revenue -- the largest source of indirect tax income in the EU -- and defending the traditional telecoms operators which are still to a large extent state-controlled.
The apparent backing of Europe's capitals could make adoption of the new rules easier, although tax questions require a unanimous vote by EU finance ministers.
The Commission is expected to adopt its proposal by the end of January. If endorsed by the finance ministers it would become law on January 1, 1999, the sources said.

The move is good news for the existing telecoms operators in the EU, who are faced with the challenge of rapid technological development and the opening of the sector to full competition in January next year.
While it spells bad news for consumers, industry sources said it was unlikely to run the emerging telecoms firms out of business or halt the downward trend in international phone calls.
"It creates more of a level playing field," Mike Corkerry, British Telecommunications's manager in European regulation, told Reuters.
"But the adjustment on the tax issue is not going to slow down the downwards pressure on international phone charges," he added.
European Telecom, a U.S. company created in the late 1980s to take advantage of Europe's high-cost international phone calls, was also undaunted by the proposal.
"Price differences will still be significant...This does not put the business at jeopardy," Joe Chtouki, marketing director of the company's Belgian operations, told Reuters.

The price of a Belgian phone call to the United States made in "call-back" was 60 percent to 70 percent cheaper than if made through the local phone company, he said. The standard VAT rate on telecoms services in the EU is about 20 percent.
